name: Manifest destiny
summary: Manifest destiny was the mid-nineteenth-century American belief that the United States was providentially destined to spread across the continent and extend republican self-government, a phrase coined by John L. O'Sullivan in 1845 and linked by the reference works to the Polk administration's annexation of Texas, the Oregon settlement and the Mexican war. It combined democratic equality among settlers, a mission to the world and claims of racial and cultural superiority, and the record is the displacement of Native American nations and the taking of Mexican lands.
scope: The mid-nineteenth-century expansionist belief as the reference and scholarly works define it (Hidalgo's and Scholnick's Encyclopedia.com entries and the American Yawp chapter), read through O'Sullivan's essays of 1839 and 1845 and his 1837 statement of the democratic principle in the review he edited, the texts those works tie to it by author and by title (the 1839 essay's editor reads his views as a synthesis of Jeffersonian republicanism, Jacksonian populism and providential history). It excludes the later overseas imperialism of 1898 and Wilsonian internationalism, which the sources treat as later expressions, and Polk's own views on tariffs, banks and the Union, which are Jacksonian Democratic positions, not the doctrine's. It was never a fixed programme, so most economic, family and social statements stay null.

notes: Themes searched in the saved sources: territory and expansion, race and the Native American nations, the Mexican war and conquest, monarchy and hereditary privilege, democracy and consent, religion and providence, progress and the past, privilege and corporations, and foreign interference. The defining sources say nothing on welfare, taxes, family, gender, the environment, technology, most civil liberties and most government statements, which stay null. Polk's 1845 inaugural address, 1845 and 1846 annual messages and 1846 war message were read (saved locally) but the defining sources do not tie them to the doctrine by title, and his tariff, bank and Union positions are Jacksonian Democratic views, so earlier answers resting on them were nulled. Supporters split on peaceful annexation and conquest and on slavery's extension; the sources record both and no statement here rests on one side.
